prompt: Review the production requirements and option data in `fixture/` and design retry handling for outbound webhooks. Write the architecture decision record to `solution/docs/design.md`, including the selected option, the alternatives, calculations, and tradeoffs. The document must contain a fenced block whose info string is exactly `decision`; its JSON must contain exactly the keys `chosen`, `options`, `limits`, and `monthly_cost_usd`. Set `chosen` to an option id, `options` to the option ids considered, and set `limits` to an object whose entries are named hard limits with `{ "limit": number, "value": number }`, using the computed value for the chosen option. Set `monthly_cost_usd` to the chosen option's monthly cost computed from the supplied price sheet.

checks.cmd: cp hidden/meta.json meta.json && mkdir -p fixture && cp -r hidden/_pristine/. fixture/ && ln -sfn . solution && node --test hidden/*.test.js

rubric.criterion: Explains why the selected durable design is preferable for this service, including operational ownership and the cost, latency, throughput, recovery, and memory tradeoffs against both alternatives. Fail: picks in-memory delay queue or gives no reason. Partial: chooses a durable option but compares only one dimension. Pass: rejects in-memory because 120,000 pending x 8 KB = 960 MB exceeds the 312 MB limit and loses retry state on a crash (RPO 5 minutes), and compares database_retry_table (about 104.54 USD, 42 s, 180/s) with external_retry_queue (about 104.42 USD, 18 s, 350/s) on cost, latency, throughput and ownership. (not code-checkable: Automated checks can verify numbers and option ids but cannot judge whether the tradeoff explanation is technically relevant, balanced, and persuasive.)

Connects the workload shape and failure behavior to an implementable retry design, including bounded scheduling, durable state, and recovery behavior. Fail: the design is generic and not tied to the workload. Partial: names durable state but not bounded scheduling or recovery. Pass: ties the 120,000 peak pending retries and the 16 KB payload (which does not constrain the choice, since all options support it) to a design with durable state, bounded batches (512 or 256 records), dispatch within the 60-second limit and at least 100/s, and states how retries resume after a restart. (not code-checkable: Tests cannot reliably assess whether the proposed architecture follows from the requirements or whether the operational reasoning is complete.)

Presents a clear, concise ADR with a traceable decision, calculations, assumptions, and follow-up safeguards that another developer could implement. Fail: the ADR is hard to follow or the calculations are missing. Partial: readable but a limit check or assumption is missing. Pass: the ADR traces the decision to the hard limits (memory under 312 MB, dispatch under 60 s, 100/s or more), shows the memory and cost arithmetic, states assumptions (such as when in-memory would fit, below about 39,000 pending), and lists follow-up safeguards another developer could implement. (not code-checkable: A script can check structure and arithmetic but cannot evaluate readability, clarity, or practical usefulness to a human developer.)

The record rejects each option it did not choose for a reason taken from the fixture (a limit, a cost, a requirement or a measurement), and states the consequence of the chosen option the team must live with. Fail: names the winner only, or rejects options for generic reasons ("too complex", "not scalable") the fixture does not support. Partial: most rejected options get a fixture-based reason, but one is waved away or the cost of the chosen option is not stated. Pass: every rejected option has a reason quoted or computed from the fixture, the chosen option's main downside is stated, and the record says what would change the decision. (code cannot check this because tests check the chosen id and the numbers, not whether each rejection is grounded)

verdicts.note: Prompt asks to design retry handling without naming which option to choose or hinting at the trap; it only specifies the output format and constraints.
All limits are clearly specified in JSON and prose; the memory calculation method (peak_records_times_payload_mb vs base_plus_batch_payload_mb) is unambiguous given the option definitions.
Fixture files provide options, limits, and prices without stating which to choose; the trap (in-memory exceeds memory) requires calculation, not direct disclosure.
Cheapest option (in-memory) fails the memory limit; choosing the correct option requires multi-file analysis and limit checking, not a trivial pick.
All necessary numbers are present; unit conventions (decimal KB/MB) are stated; the solution correctly derives memory and cost from provided data.

items.text: States that the in-memory delay queue option cannot be chosen because its memory requirement (120,000 peak pending × 8 KB = 960 MB) exceeds the retry_memory_limit_mb hard limit of 312 MB.
items.source: AWS Well-Architected Framework, https://docs.aws.amazon.com/wellarchitected/latest/framework/welcome.html (AWS copyright, idea only); idea only

items.text: Calculates monthly cost for the chosen option using the pricing.json rates: database_retry_table costs 104.54 USD/month (2 compute units at $52, 1.2 GB storage at $0.22/GB, 3 GB backup at $0.08/GB, 8M requests at $0.005/M); external_retry_queue costs 104.42 USD/month (2 worker units at $52, 1 GB storage at $0.30/GB, 8M requests at $0.015/M).
Explains that the 16 KB maximum_payload_kb from traffic.json is a distractor that does not constrain option choice since all three options support at least 16 KB payloads.

Verifies that the chosen option satisfies all hard limits: memory under 312 MB, dispatch latency under 60 seconds (database: 42s, external: 18s), and throughput at least 100/s (database: 180/s, external: 350/s).
items.source: Google SRE Book, https://sre.google/sre-book/table-of-contents/ (CC BY-NC-ND 4.0); idea only

items.text: Discusses the operational tradeoff between database_retry_table (lower cost by $0.12/month, simpler ownership if the service already owns a database) and external_retry_queue (lower latency 18s vs 42s, higher throughput 350/s vs 180/s, managed service reduces operational complexity).
items.source: Google SRE Book, https://sre.google/sre-book/table-of-contents/ (CC BY-NC-ND 4.0); idea only

items.text: Addresses failure mode: the in-memory option would lose all retry state on process crash or container restart, violating the RPO requirement of max 5 minutes, whereas both database and external queue options persist state.
items.source: Google SRE Book, https://sre.google/sre-book/table-of-contents/ (CC BY-NC-ND 4.0); idea only

items.text: Notes that the 512 batch_records for database_retry_table and 256 batch_records for external_retry_queue are in-memory batch sizes for dispatch, not peak storage, and that the memory_model determines how to calculate actual memory consumption.
States that if peak pending retries dropped below ~39,000 records, the in-memory option would fit within the memory limit, changing the decision calculus.

weakAnswers: picks the in-memory delay queue as the cheapest option ($0/month) without checking whether it satisfies the memory limit
calculates memory incorrectly as 120,000 × 8 bytes instead of 120,000 × 8 KB, concluding that in-memory fits
rejects the external_retry_queue because its 256 batch_records is smaller than the database's 512, confusing batch size with capacity
chooses database_retry_table solely because it has better RPO (1 min) and RTO (18 min) than required, without checking throughput
picks external_retry_queue as the only valid option without recognizing database_retry_table also satisfies all constraints
